How I designed and launched the world's first interactive television multiplayer games as a founding team member of Two Way TV, earning a BAFTA nomination along the way.

Founding team member and product design lead for the world's first interactive television gaming network — built before smartphones, before streaming, and before anyone had a name for what we were doing.
Build compelling real-time multiplayer game experiences within the severe technical and latency constraints of 1990s digital television broadcast infrastructure.
Two Way TV / Two Way Media
Interactive game design, development, and broadcast deployment across Sky Digital, cable, and international platforms in the US, Canada, and Australia

Two Way TV was a world-leading interactive television pioneer — operating dedicated gaming channels across the UK's major digital platforms and licensing the technology internationally. The company held key interactive TV patents and signed a strategic alliance with Microsoft to bring the platform to the MSTV standard. I joined as a founding team member in 1995, when interactive television was still largely theoretical. I worked across the full stack as designer and developer simultaneously — in an era when that distinction barely existed — spending eight years designing and building the products that proved the medium was real.
The UK's first head-to-head multiplayer game.

In November 2001, Two Way TV launched Fruity4some on the nti digital cable service — the UK's first head-to-head interactive multiplayer game on cable television. Players could challenge other subscribers in real time, from the same household or across the network, with in-game chat, live leaderboards, and a pay-to-play model that established a template for interactive entertainment billing. I designed the game interaction model and the full television user experience, navigating remote-control interaction constraints with no established design language to draw from.
UK's first head-to-head interactive multiplayer game on digital cable. Real-time gameplay, in-game chat, and leaderboards — all navigated with a TV remote.
Fruity4some multiplayer game running on Two Way TV's cable service, showing the fruit-grid gameplay, player names, timer, and chat prompt
Armchair Manager — sport meets broadcast interactivity.

Before Fruity4some, I produced 'Armchair Manager – Football' — a real-time interactive sports experience that put viewers in the manager's seat during live Sky Sports coverage. Players made tactical decisions synced to actual match events, with outcomes tied to what happened on the pitch. Interactive television had never been used this way: not as an overlay on content, but as a parallel experience woven into a live broadcast. The product earned a BAFTA Interactive Entertainment Award nomination in 2000, recognising it as a pioneering advance in broadcast interactivity.
Two Way TV interactive television game interface
A platform that predicted the future of interactive media.

Two Way TV operated at a scale and ambition that few appreciated at the time. The technology that underpinned our games — real-time bidirectional communication over broadcast infrastructure, audience participation systems, second-screen interaction models — was years ahead of the mainstream. The strategic alliance with Microsoft, the international licensing, the granted patents: these were signals of an industry trying to catch up with what we'd already built. The direct line from that work to modern interactive streaming, second-screen experiences, and broadcast gamification is not subtle.

Upwave was Turner's IoT-driven digital health venture, exploring the intersection of quantified-self data and personalized content. As Vice President, Product & UX, I led the specialized teams responsible for taking the venture from concept to market. Partnering with IDEO for initial market validation, I established the product strategy and introduced a lean methodology that enabled daily release cycles, accelerating growth to 1M monthly unique users in just eight months.
An ecosystem of content, challenges, and analytics.
I directed the product roadmap and user experience strategy across the entire Upwave ecosystem, guiding teams to ensure a seamless integration between media consumption and health tracking behaviors.
Directed the UX strategies for a responsive media platform built to drive engagement and recirculation.

Oversaw the design framework for multi-day wellness challenges, applying behavioral science to daily progress tracking.

Building a platform at the forefront of quantified-self technology (pre-Apple Watch) required rigorous methodology. I initiated a partnership with IDEO to secure product-market fit and validate key assumptions before large-scale investment. Working cross-functionally, I led the transition of the teams to a lean product methodology, establishing a cadence of daily release cycles that increased platform recirculation from 5% to 24%.
Directed the UX and product teams to establish the foundational information architecture and component strategy.
Managed multidisciplinary teams ensuring complex health data intersections were logically translated into accessible interfaces.

Prior to leading Upwave, my tenure at Turner included serving as Senior Director of Innovation & Emerging Technology spanning CNN, Cartoon Network, TBS & TNT. I led multi-disciplinary R&D teams that pioneered early mobile augmented reality applications and the sync-to-TV technology that ultimately won a Primetime Emmy Award. These efforts resulted in two granted U.S. patents for automatic content recognition. I also collaborated on the design of the CNN 'Magic Wall,' introducing a massive multi-touch paradigm that redefined data storytelling across the broadcast industry.
